label: paragraph_title
text: HONG KONG'S POSITION.

label: paragraph_title
text: IMPROVEMENT SINCE THE BOYCOTT.

label: text
text: OVERSEAS MONEY FOR PROPERTY: "NOT DEVOID OF HOPE."

label: text
text: Hong Kong's trade position has improved since the "settlement of the boycott." After extensive inquiries the situation vis-à-vis Canton is "summed up as "not devoid of hope."

label: text
text: In spite of agitation and intimidation, I can state on the best authority that at least $3,000,000 worth of "piece" goods has been sent from Hong Kong to Canton since Oct. 10, when the blockade of this Colony was voluntarily called off by the Strike Committee.

label: text
text: Much has been said about the restrictions to trade through the boycott not having completely ended, but from investigations I have made, I have come to the conclusion that a good deal of the recent impprovement in the Colony has been directly or indirectly attributable to the settlement.

label: text
text: In Nam: Pak Hong the sugar market has had a small boom now that former outlets have been reopened. Not only are the products of the two local refineries exported from Hong Kong but large quantities of raw sugar are transhipped here to the two Kwang provinces and other parts of China.

label: text
text: The property market has shown signs of a new lease of life but the hapse of the Rents Restriction Ordinance and other causes have also contributed.

label: paragraph_title
text: Effect of the Dollar.

label: text
text: Metals and other foreign manufactures have found their way up to Canton, Wuchow, &c., as I saw on making a trip this week at the invitation of the “China Mail.” “While some trades have been adversely affected by the slump in the dollar, others have received benefit.

label: text
text: Gold currencies having gone up, Chinese emigrants are remitting more money home, mostly through exchange banks in Hong Kong. Shops known as “California” dealers have done more business now that intercourse has been resumed with the interior.

label: paragraph_title
text: Good Sign of the Times.

label: text
text: Good trade in Malaya and other places down South has resulted in more money, earned by overseas Chinese, being sent back to Hong Kong.

label: text
text: This week there were several inquiries by brokers, on behalf of principals returned from Singapore, for Chinese house property situated on the central Praya.

label: text
text: Obviously such premises are required for business purposes—a very desirable sign of the times.

label: text
text: Because landlords are not now encumbered by law and are at liberty to retrieve possession, there is now inducement for merchants to buy property for their own accommodation, in preference to paying higher rentals elsewhere.

label: paragraph_title
text: Abundance of Money?

label: text
text: House owners have been able to increase rents, thereby enhancing the relative value. Some of those who secured mortgages during the boom have now found buyers who paid enough to let them wipe off the loans.

label: text
text: It is not strictly correct to say that money is plentiful. The absence of other forms of investment has deflected funds (in the hands of native bankers) to the property market.

label: text
text: Interest on mortgage has lowered slightly but there is no hard and fast rate. Quotations vary somewhat: Short terms and long margins command low rates. Advances are worked out in ratio to the desirability of the security so that fairly high-interest will have to be offered on suburban lots.

label: paragraph_title
text: Feeling of Restraint.

label: text
text:
Exchange fluctuations and uncertainty as to the future have jointly mitigated against new business in the piece goods market. But when the blockade was lifted, dealers in both Canton and Hong Kong did their best to replenish the very low stocks in Canton.
Mostly in fiscal shipments, lots have been shipped up to meet the autumn and winter requirements in Canton, but a feeling of restraint available.
This uneasiness is not due entirely to the threat that British goods will not be handled after Nov. 8. Having satisfied the first rush so to speak, dealers are waiting for the next development before further committing themselves. Such prudence can hardly be deplored.

label: text
text: Hardware and metals have also had outlets so that the market is not so stagnant as a month ago.

label: text
text:
Merchants Own Interests.
The threat of the Transport Union in Canton to "strike" against British trade as from Monday has caused considerable alarm in both ports. Merchants are looking forward, not without confidence, to the Nationalist (or Provincial). Government to take the initiative should a deadlock ensue. The situation is not devoid of hope.

label: text
text: To the traders themselves, those engaged in commerce are looking for means to tide over the agitation to sever economic relations at a future date. The circular forbidding searchers and/or pickets from entering shops is an indication that the Canton merchants are alive to preserving their own interests.

label: paragraph_title
text: NOT SCOTSMEN

label: text
text: EGYPTIAN RATHER THAN BE

label: text
text: K.O.S.B. "BOMBSHELL."

label: text
text: Scotsmen prefer to be Egyptians than Englishmen or Americans!

label: text
text: Such was the startling discovery made by a Highlander while riding on a lower level tram in Hong Kong.

label: text
text: There were two young men who hotly denied that they were Sassenachs or Yankees and, ex-asperated, pronounced themselves to be "natives of Egypt. They were two privates of the 2nd. King's Own Scottish Borderers, the new infantry regiment on the station.

label: text
text: The Tramway Co. extends to men in the Services the right of paying half-fare while travelling in uniform. Men of foreign Armies and Navies are debarred. Under Suspicion.

label: text
text: If the two Privates concerned see this, they must excuse the conductor who, although plainly tactless and ignorant of military pageant, was merely doing his duty. Men in uniform, who were neither in the British Army or Navy, had proferred ten cents in the past and unknowingly pocketed five cents change till a European inspector happened to examine the ticket.

label: text
text: This conductor was trying to ascertain if the two Scottish soldiers were in the British forces, evidently viewing with suspicion the tarant trews they wore. He particularly disliked their Glengarry caps which, in his humble opinion, too "closely resembled the "hat of disgrace" mated out to the vixen-foccd, white-bearded villain of the Chinese stage type of mandarin.

label: text
text:
The Good Sembritan.
His vocabulary did not include the word British so he asked, when offered ten cents for two first-class fares: — "You Engish?"

label: text
text:
"No," returned the Privates with sorrow plainly written on their young faces.
In a moment of inspiration, the conductor rejoined: "You, the American?"

label: text
text: “No, we are Egyptian,” roared one of the couple but further trouble was saved when a gentle man who was on the train and had overheard the conversation went to the rescue.

label: paragraph_title

label: paragraph_title
text: Should They Accept a Lift?

label: text
text: WEEKLY SHANGHAI LETTER.

label: text
text: Chatty Notes From Clubland:

label: text
text:
Shanghai, Oct. 30.
When a car draws up by the roadside and the "well-dressed young man" driving the car offers "two office girls" a lift, what is the correct procedure of the "two office girls" aforesaid?

label: text
text: This conundrum has virtually set the whole town talking. It started in this way: "Two Office Girls" wrote a letter seeking the advice of the Editor of the "North-China Daily News" upon the problem. That august personage published a said letter in the correspondence columns of the "North-China Daily News" under the appropriate caption of William of Wykeham's well-known maxim, "Manners Makyth Man." The columns of "the Old Lady of the Bund" have been crowded out with letters on the subject which has also formed the chief topic of conversation in the clubs and city hostelries.

label: paragraph_title
text: "Fust" or Prudés?

label: text
text: Summing up the question in "a leading article, the Editor of "the "North-China Daily News" states that the following solutions emerge: The girls should smile sweetly and accept, but if they do they dub themselves either fast or foolish. They should turn haughtily away and refuse with disdain, but if they do they dub themselves prudes and/or early Victorians. Most people agree with Mr. O. M. Green in that we have derived no great soft from the discussion, and the correspondence has been quite right closed.

Taking the route over hilly country, they took this railway town without any difficulty and shot northwards, moving nearly 40 miles in one night.

label: text

label: paragraph_title

label: text
text:
The experiences of a passenger who returned to the Colony from Wuchow by the s.s. "Tai Ming," one of the first vessels to make the trip since Nov. 1—the day the much discussed new taxes were announced to come into force—throw some light upon the actual situation on the West River.
The “China Mail” is informed that the “Tai Ming” left Hong Kong on the afternoon of Nov. 1, being escorted, as usual, from Wangmoon to the Cliff.
Upon arrival at Samshui on the following morning, they found a Nationalist two-funnel gunboat at anchor opposite the Customs Buildings, H.M.S. “Moorhen” lying an anchor nearby.
The Chinese gunboat had one buoy, apparently made of a kerosene tin, painted red and surmounted by a red flag, moored about 120 ft. ahead of her, another the same distance, astern with two others, one on either side, approximately 75 feet from the gunboat.

label: text
text: A "Nationalist armed launch, which was escorting a passenger motor-boat was fired upon by the gunboat for passing too close to the outer buoy.

label: text
text: Just before the voyage was continued, the Customs received orders, apparently from Headquarters at Peking, not to allow the new dues collectors to interfere with the rightful Customs officials and masters of British vessels received instructions from the Naval authority not to allow any of the Nationalist officials to board their ships.

label: text
text: On the return trip, two and a half days later, it was found that Nationalist officials had commandeered some out-buildings belonging to the Customs. The latter had communicated with Peking and received instructions to throw out the intruders—instructions which were promptly carried out. The arrival of H.M.S. "Robin" apparently had some effect upon the Nationalist officials, for, beyond a display of flags, nothing has been done.
